units.translation: from where they approved calling the people Curetes
by the report of the local people
Thus I emended for ὁ λεύκασπις λαὸς εὐτρεπής [the white-shielded ready people] (or εὐπρεπής [comely]).
This great people flows forth, a vanguard of horsemen
For all the horse-driving and land-treading people
let them come, and when he comes, the people honor him greatly
so that the people may be bitten
Attic (or urban, as at v. 997, Hermann) people
for from the beginning the people are fond of blame
Thus Musgravius for λέπαδνον [yoke-strap]. Of this form there is only this one example: more frequent from Homer onward is άλαπαδνός [weak].
seeing him never boasting, weak in helpless miseries
to empty out; hence to plunder, to sack
properly to empty out; hence to plunder, to sack
They explain it by ἐκκενοῦν [to empty out]: Athenaeus 8 p. 362f., Hesychius and other grammarians indicated in the Thesaurus vol. 5 p. 109.
where the scholiast has ἐκκενώσειν, ἀπὸ τοῦ λαπάθου [to empty out, from the dock].

where Triclinius has Μοῖρα λαπάξει [Fate will sack], a form which the tragedians perhaps did not use except when the meter demanded it, just as they seem to have preferred ἀμαυροῦν [to weaken] to the other form μαυροῦν [to weaken] when the meter allowed. Add to this that ἀλαπάζω [to sack] is a Homeric form.
they swore an oath that they would sack the city of the Cadmeans by force, laying waste to it
and Fate will sack all the flocks from the towers
to empty out, from the dock

Thus Wieseler for λάμπαι [moulds] (λάμπα [mould] Canterus), since in other writers too it is usually written λάμπη [mould], on which see the Thesaurus vol. 5 p. 82 and 111, where see what is said about the proper meaning of the word: ὁ παχὺς ἀφρὸς ὁ ἐπιπολάζων τῷ οἴνῳ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ὑγροῖς [the thick foam that floats on wine and other liquids].
the thick foam that floats on wine and other liquids
to utter a sound, to speak, to cry out
to utter a sound, to speak, to cry out
The aorist is λακεῖν [to have cried out]
Of the perfect λέλακα [I have cried out] (with the middle syllable lengthened) there is one example
one from one place, another from another, they raised a cry throughout the city
uttering another evil woe upon the house
the naves of the heavy-laden axles creaked
such boasting is not shameful for a noble woman to utter
from the depths it uttered a cry in the dead of night
and the judges of these dreams spoke from the gods
they uttered every word through justice (or according to justice, Hermann)
and already the whole land has cried out in grief
I would not exchange my misfortune for your servitude
